verses.translation_literal: And it was, at the end of two years of days, and Pharaoh [was] dreaming, and behold, [he was] standing by the Nile.
verses.translation_dramatic: Two years had turned over in the dark, and Joseph lay forgotten in the prison. Then, one night, Pharaoh slept, and the sleep took him down to the river. He was standing on the bank of the Nile, in the hush before the dawn.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter opens on a stretch of time with no event in it: 'two years of days'. The odd phrase 'years of days' is read by Rashbam as two complete years, not a year and a day. The count starts where the last chapter ended, with the butler forgetting Joseph, so the silence is the point. Note the participles: Pharaoh 'is dreaming' and 'is standing' – the Hebrew puts us inside the dream as it happens, where the KJV's 'dreamed' and 'he stood' narrate it from a safe distance.

The KJV adds 'full' and 'came to pass'; neither is in the Hebrew. For Pharaoh, standing at the Nile is no scenery: Egypt lives or dies by its annual flood, and the king is the guarantor of that flood. Rashi notes that only the Nile is called a ye'or in Hebrew, since Egypt's land is cut with channels fed from it. Direct the actor as a man at the source of his country's life.

philological_notes.note: The word for the Nile and its canals, an Egyptian-sounding word, not the usual Hebrew nahar 'river'. It marks the scene as Egyptian and the river as the source of grain and hunger alike.
'From the end of two years of days'. 'Days' stands for whole years, so a full two years is meant.

verses.translation_literal: And behold, from the Nile coming up seven cows, good of appearance and fat of flesh, and they grazed in the reed-grass.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there, out of the water, they came: seven cows, rising one after another from the Nile, sleek and lovely to look at, their flanks heavy with flesh. They climbed the bank and settled into the green reeds, and they grazed.
verses.directors_commentary:
'Behold' is the dream's own camera: the audience sees what Pharaoh sees, suddenly. The cows rise from the river, and the actor must play the wonder of it, since in Egypt cattle and the Nile both carried divine associations, which makes this picture natural for a king's dream.

The KJV's 'kine' is archaic, and 'meadow' is a guess at 'achu: Rashi says marsh, Ramban says the grass that grows on riverbanks. 'Well favoured' is fine, but 'fatfleshed' hides that the Hebrew uses the same two words for appearance and flesh again and again, so that the good and the bad cows are a matched set of opposites. Rashi reads the beauty as a sign of the years of plenty, when no creature envies another.

philological_notes.note: Reed-grass or marsh vegetation by the water, a rare word. Rashi takes it as marsh, Ramban as the grass growing on riverbanks.

verses.translation_literal: And behold, seven cows, other ones, coming up after them from the Nile, bad of appearance and thin of flesh; and they stood beside the cows upon the lip of the Nile.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, behind them, more. Seven other cows hauled themselves up out of the Nile, and the sight of them was wrong: bad to look at, thin in the flesh, the bones near the surface. They did not graze. They came up the bank and stood, close beside the sleek cows, at the very lip of the river.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Nile is Egypt's whole economy, and a cow rising from it is no oddity to an Egyptian eye: the river's annual flood is what fills the granaries, and cattle are wealth. So the horror here is not the animals but the order of them. The second herd rises after the first and does not wait its turn behind them; it takes its place at their side, standing, on the same bank.

The KJV's "kine" and "ill favoured" are archaic where the Hebrew is blunt: ra'ot mar'eh is simply "bad of appearance," the ordinary word for bad, and daqqot basar is "thin of flesh." The KJV has "stood by the other kine upon the brink," which is fair; the Hebrew says "the lip of the Nile," a body image the English keeps only faintly. Note too that the verb is vata'amodenah, "and they stood." It is not "and they fed," as with the first herd. Radak makes exactly this point: the text did not say they grazed, but that they stood next to the first, and he takes this to be part of the dream's clarity. Ramban reads the closeness, "beside them," as a sign that there would be no interval between the seven years of plenty and the seven of famine. Sforno reads it differently: standing together before the eating means that famine and plenty would exist side by side at one time, as in 41:54, "there was famine in all lands, but in all the land of Egypt there was bread." Play the actors' stillness: the thin cows do nothing yet, and that is the threat.

philological_notes.note: The feminine plural of the common adjective "bad," here agreeing with the cows. It describes how they look ("bad of appearance"), not what they do. The same form recurs for the thin cows in 41:4.
"And they stood," with the rare feminine-plural -nah ending. The verb is stationary, not a verb of grazing; Radak points this out, and Ramban and Sforno draw different lessons from the closeness.

The Nile, in a word that Hebrew took from Egyptian (itrw). The text uses it of the Nile throughout Genesis 41 and Exodus 1-8, never of an ordinary river, so "the river" in English loses a proper name.

verses.translation_literal: And the cows, bad of appearance and thin of the flesh, ate [obj] the seven cows, good of appearance and the fat ones; and Pharaoh awoke.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the thin cows ate. They ate the seven that were lovely to look at, the seven that were heavy with flesh, and the river bank held no sound but that. Then Pharaoh woke.
verses.directors_commentary:
The shock is in the verb. "Ate" is the ordinary word for eating, used for the feeding of livestock and of people alike, and the scene turns on it: the lean herd consumes the sleek one, and nothing is said beyond that. Do not play the moment as a roar. The text does not decorate it.

The KJV has "did eat up," which adds a finality the Hebrew leaves to the verb alone, and "So Pharaoh awoke," where the Hebrew has only "and Pharaoh awoke": the little "So" invents a consequence. The Hebrew also repeats the very words of the first description, ra'ot mar'eh and daqqot basar, now as a title worn by the eaters, set against yefot mar'eh and beri'ot for the eaten, so that the two herds are weighed in the same terms. Rashi hears a sign here that all the joy of plenty will be forgotten in the days of famine. Ramban dissents from Rashi and takes the eating as the years of famine consuming the years of plenty, which is Radak's reading too. Rashbam adds that Pharaoh wakes and sleeps at once: the dream comes in two parts, with a short waking between them.

philological_notes.note: "And he awoke," a verb used for waking from sleep or dream (also Gen 9:24, 28:16). It marks the break between the two dreams; Rashbam says Pharaoh did not yet know it was a dream.
"And the fat ones," the feminine plural of the adjective bari', "healthy, plump" (well-fed). It has nothing to do with the verb bara', "to create," though the consonants look alike.

verses.translation_literal: And he slept and dreamed a second time, and behold, seven ears of grain coming up on one stalk, fat and good.
verses.translation_dramatic: But sleep came for him again, and with it a second dream. Now it was a field he saw: seven ears of grain rising together on a single stalk, heavy, golden, whole.
verses.directors_commentary:
He goes back to sleep, and Hebrew gives it three quick verbs: slept, dreamed, a second time. The second dream is the first in another form: cows for the plough, grain for the harvest, the two halves of Egypt's farming year. Ramban takes the cows as the sign of ploughing and the ears as the sign of reaping.

The KJV's 'corn' means grain in general (wheat or barley), not maize, and 'rank' meant lush, not foul, which sounds wrong to a modern ear. The Hebrew repeats the same word for the good cows and the good ears (beri'ot, 'fat'), so the dreams rhyme. Rashbam sees in the single stalk a sign of how abundant the plenty would be.

philological_notes.note: 'Ears of grain'. The same word later gives the famous test-word 'shibboleth'. Ibn Ezra comments on its masculine plural form with feminine adjectives.
'Fat, healthy': the same word that described the good cows in verse 2, so the dreams are linked by repetition.

verses.translation_literal: And behold, seven ears of grain, thin and scorched by an east wind, sprouting after them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there, behind them, sprang up seven more: thin, shrunken, dry, scorched by the wind that blows out of the eastern desert, withered before they had ripened.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'east wind' (qadim) is the hot desert wind from the east, which in Egypt and Canaan can wither a crop within days. For a farmer in Egypt this is the real enemy, and it is why the dream of ears has a more concrete menace than the cows. The Hebrew word is also 'the front', since the east is where the sun rises, which is Ibn Ezra's explanation.

The KJV's 'blasted' is a good older word but is no longer clear. 'Sprung up' is right: the verb is tzamach, a sprouting, and Ramban notes that Pharaoh does not see them grow, only that they stand there after the others, as in a still picture. As with the cows, the bad comes up after the good.

philological_notes.note: The east wind, the hot dry desert wind; also 'the front', the direction of sunrise.
'Scorched, blasted' (of grain, by wind or blight). Rashi connects it to the Aramaic of Onkelos shekifan.

verses.translation_literal: And the thin ears of grain swallowed the seven ears of grain, the fat and the full; and Pharaoh awoke, and behold, a dream.
verses.translation_dramatic: The thin ears gaped, and swallowed the seven full ears whole. Pharaoh woke again, and as the dark room steadied around him, he understood: it was a dream. Only a dream. And yet it would not let him go.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb changes. In verse 4 the cows 'ate'; here the ears 'swallowed' (bala'), a word of gulping, of the earth swallowing Korah. Hebrew escalates, and the KJV's 'devoured' does not mark it. The dream does not explain how an ear of grain swallows; it simply does.

The last words, 'and behold, a dream', are the KJV's 'and, behold, it was a dream', with 'it was' added. Hebrew keeps it bare: the same 'behold' that introduced every vision in the dream now introduces the waking recognition. Rashi says the dream was now complete and needed interpreters. Ramban notes Pharaoh treats the two dreams as one dream, and that he lay awake until morning, hoping for more.

philological_notes.note: 'Swallowed whole', stronger than 'ate' in verse 4; a verb of gulping down, used elsewhere for the earth swallowing Korah's company.
'And behold, a dream': Pharaoh sees that it was a dream only after waking. Rashbam compares 'and behold, it was Leah'.

verses.translation_literal: And it was in the morning, and his spirit was struck, and he sent and called all the chartummim of Egypt and all its wise men; and Pharaoh recounted to them his dream, and there was none interpreting them for Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: Morning came, and the light did not quiet him. His spirit beat inside him like a struck bell. He sent his messengers out and summoned every diviner-priest in Egypt and every sage of the land, and in the great hall Pharaoh told them his dream. They listened. They said nothing that would hold.
verses.directors_commentary:
'His spirit was troubled' is milder than the Hebrew. The verb pa'am means to strike or to beat, and Rashi pictures the spirit clanging in him like a bell (pa'amon). This is a king who cannot sit still. Rashi and Ramban compare Nebuchadnezzar, whose spirit is likewise 'struck' in Daniel 2:1.

The KJV's 'magicians' for chartummim is acceptable but vague: these are the sacred scribes and priests of the Egyptian temples, who kept the books of omens and dreams. Ibn Ezra calls them the experts in nature and the stars; Rashi links the word to the bones of the dead, consulted for answers, an etymology I would not rely on. Pharaoh gathers the whole establishment, 'all' and 'all', and none of it works.

The last clause is open: 'there was none interpreting them'. Rashi says the interpreters did interpret, but nothing that suited Pharaoh. Radak and Sforno read it as no real interpretation at all. The KJV's 'none that could interpret' chooses the second.

philological_notes.note: 'Was struck, was knocked about'; the same root as pa'am 'a beat, a time' and pa'amon 'bell'. The spirit is physically jolted.
Egyptian temple priest-scribes who handled sacred writings, omens and magic. The word is foreign; Ibn Ezra says Aramaic or Egyptian.
'No one interpreting them': the plural 'them' (the dreams) after a singular 'dream' is noted by commentators.

verses.translation_literal: And the chief of the cupbearers spoke with Pharaoh, saying: My sins I [am] causing to be remembered today.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the chief of the cupbearers stepped forward out of the silence and spoke to the king. 'My sins,' he said. 'Today I must bring my sins to mind.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The man who held Pharaoh's cup speaks up, and what he says first is a confession. The KJV's 'I do remember my faults' softens twice: chata'ai is 'my sins', a word of failing the king, not a slip; and the verb is a causative, 'I cause to be remembered', so he is bringing them up on purpose, not merely recalling them. Radak says it is unseemly to remind a king of one's offences after pardon, so the butler speaks only because the king needs it. Sforno hears a man who does not blame the king for the prison: it was his own fault.

There is also an ironic echo: the butler is now the one who 'remembers' (zakar), after two years in which he did not remember Joseph (40:23). He does not say that yet. Direct him as a courtier who must make a request sound like a service, and who is slightly embarrassed.

philological_notes.note: Causative of 'remember': to mention, to bring to mind. It is the opposite of what he did to Joseph in 40:23, where he 'did not remember' him.
'My sins/offences': in a courtly setting, failures against the king.

verses.translation_literal: Pharaoh was angry with his servants, and put me in custody in the house of the chief of the slaughterers, me and the chief of the bakers.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'Pharaoh was angry with his servants. He gave me over to the guard in the house of the captain of the executioners: me, and the chief of the bakers with me.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The butler speaks about the king in the third person, as courtiers do: 'Pharaoh was angry', not 'you were angry'. Ibn Ezra and Rashbam both discuss this etiquette. He also makes his own offence collective: Pharaoh was angry with 'his servants', as if the cause lay in the whole household. A careful man.

The KJV's 'wroth' is archaic. 'Captain of the guard' is a respectable translation of sar hatabbachim, but the word is literally 'chief of the slaughterers' (tabbach is a butcher or cook), which is why YLT has 'executioners'. The title could mean the head of the royal guard whose duty included executions, which is a more menacing house to be locked in. 'Ward' in KJV is also obsolete. The repeated 'me' ('otti... 'otti) is pointed: Ibn Ezra and Radak say this is ordinary Hebrew repetition.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'chief of the slaughterers/butchers'; used for the commander of the royal guard, who also carried out executions. The same title Potiphar bears in chapters 37 and 39.
'Me' said twice: ordinary Hebrew repetition for emphasis and for bringing the baker in.

verses.translation_literal: And we dreamed a dream in one night, I and he; each according to the interpretation of his dream we dreamed.
verses.translation_dramatic: 'One night we dreamed, the baker and I, each of us a dream. And each dream, as it turned out, was shaped to its meaning.'
verses.directors_commentary:
The butler now tells the story of the prison dreams, quickly and a little defensively. 'I and he' is the baker, whom he does not name; the butler is the survivor, and his tone should show it.

The last clause is awkward in the KJV, which copies the word order: 'we dreamed each man according to the interpretation of his dream'. The sense is that each dream was fitted to its own interpretation, so the interpretation proved true. Rashi reads it as a dream suited to the meaning it was given; Ramban takes it as the dreams being different and having different meanings, so no one confuses them with one dream. This matters for Pharaoh, whose experts cannot do what this prisoner did.

philological_notes.note: 'According to the interpretation of his dream': the dream matched its meaning. Rashi: the dream was suited to the interpretation given.

verses.translation_literal: And there [was] with us a lad, a Hebrew, a slave to the chief of the slaughterers; and we recounted to him, and he interpreted for us our dreams; each man according to his dream he interpreted.
verses.translation_dramatic: And there was a young man there with us in the prison, a Hebrew, a slave of the captain of the guard. We told him what we had seen, and he gave us the meaning of our dreams. To each man he spoke the meaning that fitted his own dream.
verses.directors_commentary:
The butler speaks before the king and has to describe a man he has barely thought of in two years. Notice how he lists him: lad, Hebrew, slave, in that order, with the master named last. For a court official, each word lowers the man. In Genesis, "Hebrew" is mostly how Egyptians speak of Joseph (39:14, 39:17, and here at 41:12) and Joseph himself uses it when speaking to Egyptians (40:15); it can mark an outsider before Egyptians. Rashi takes the three words together as contempt, and hears "lad" as a fool unfit for greatness. Radak is gentler: "lad" because he waited on them in the prison, and "slave of the captain" so that Pharaoh could ask the captain about him by name.

The KJV's "servant" for 'eved softens it. The Hebrew word is "slave," the same word Pharaoh's "servants" bear in 41:10, and this is a man whose owner sits in the court. "Captain of the guard" is also a loose rendering of sar hatabbachim, whose root word means slaughterer or cook; the office likely began in the royal kitchen and extended to the king's bodyguard. The close of the verse repeats "interpret": he interpreted to us our dreams, each man according to his dream he interpreted. Rashi, Radak and Ramban each read the final phrase a little differently; the simplest sense is that each man got an interpretation of his own dream, as the outcome in 41:13 will prove.

philological_notes.note: "Hebrew." In Genesis it is mostly used by Egyptians of Joseph (39:14, 39:17, 41:12), and Joseph uses it himself to Egyptians (40:15); it is also Abram's label in 14:13. Rashi hears contempt in the butler's list of lad, Hebrew, slave.
"Lad," a young man of service age, not a child; Radak says the butler chose the word because Joseph attended them in the prison. Rashi takes it as a slight.
"Each according to his dream." Radak supplies a missing "to" ("to each man"); Ramban prefers that each man's interpretation matched his own dream's future.

verses.translation_literal: And it was, just as he interpreted for us, so it was: me he returned upon my station, and him he hanged.
verses.translation_dramatic: And it fell out just as he had said. Everything he told us came to pass. Me, they set back in my place. And the other, the baker, was hanged.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the butler's whole case in one breath: the interpreter is proved by his results. The structure is stark. "Me" and "him" are both pushed to the front of their clauses (otí, otó), so the two fates stand side by side like weights on a scale, and the verbs are as short as they can be: he returned, he hanged.

In both Hebrew and the KJV the subject of "he restored" and "he hanged" is left unnamed; the KJV's "he" is as open as the Hebrew's. Whoever hears it, Pharaoh included, can supply the name; the butler does not say it.

The KJV's "mine office" suits the Hebrew kanni, which literally means a base or stand: the place where a man stands. "Hanged" is the right English verb for talah, but it needs care: the Hebrew verb means to hang or suspend, and for a body after death, which is what 40:19 foretold and 40:22 reports. The butler does not describe the method. For the court, what matters is the one-to-one match: a restored butler, a dead baker, exactly as interpreted.

philological_notes.note: "My station, my base," from kēn, a stand or base. It means the place where one stands to serve; Onkelos renders it "my service" (shimmushi), which fits the butler's cup-bearing office.

"He hanged," literally "he hung up." It is used here and in 40:19, 40:22 of the baker's body displayed after death. The verse gives no method; the English "hanged" can suggest a noose, which the Hebrew does not say.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh sent and called Joseph, and they rushed him from the pit; and he shaved and changed his garments, and he came to Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pharaoh sent, and Joseph was summoned. They ran him up out of the pit, out of the dark and the stink, with no time to waste. He was shaved, he put off the clothes of the prison and put on clean ones, and he stepped into the presence of Pharaoh.
verses.directors_commentary: The speed is the first thing to play. The verb is a causative of 'run': nobody walks Joseph anywhere. A king's summons cannot wait, and Radak adds that the matter is urgent. Then comes the slow, ceremonial part: no one stands before Pharaoh unkempt. Egyptians shaved head and face and kept clean linen, and Joseph, a Semite from Canaan, must be made to look like a man the court can look at. Rashi, citing Genesis Rabbah, says he shaved out of respect for the monarchy, and Sforno notes that one does not come to the king's gate in sackcloth. Note the irony the KJV 'dungeon' blurs: the Hebrew is bor, 'pit', the very word used for the empty cistern where his brothers threw him (37:20-24). Rashi explains that it names a prison dug like a hole in the ground. Joseph goes from one pit to a throne. The KJV's 'hastily' is fine; its 'dungeon' loses the echo.

philological_notes.note: 'The pit', the word for the cistern in Genesis 37 and here for the prison. Rashi says even a pit without water is called bor.
Causative of 'run', with an impersonal plural subject: 'they made him run'. Radak ties the haste to the urgency of the king's word.
'He shaved'. Rashi: out of respect for the royal court. Egyptians were clean-shaven and Semites were typically bearded.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh said to Joseph: A dream I dreamed, and an interpreter there is none for it; and I, I have heard about you, saying: you hear a dream to interpret it.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, 'I have dreamed a dream, and there is no one to read it. But I have heard of you, I have heard it said: when you hear a dream, you can open it.'
verses.directors_commentary: Pharaoh opens with the thing he cannot do: he has a dream and no interpreter. He is a god-king asking a foreign prisoner for help, so the sentence is a confession wrapped in a compliment. The Hebrew piles up the sound of dreaming, 'a dream I dreamed' (chalom chalamti), and the KJV's flatter 'I have dreamed a dream' is right to keep it. The word 'and I, I' (va'ani) puts Pharaoh himself in the foreground against the failed experts. Joseph's reputation is carried by the verb 'you hear'. The KJV softens this to 'canst understand'; the Hebrew says 'you hear a dream', and Rashi and Radak gloss shama' here as 'understand', as in 'a nation whose language you will not hear' (Deut. 28:49). A modern audience would hear it as the ear of a specialist: Joseph takes a dream in as the physician takes in a pulse.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'you hear', here 'you comprehend'. Rashi and Radak both read it as understanding and cite 'a nation whose language you will not hear' (Deut 28:49).
A cognate accusative, 'a dream I dreamed'. The repetition marks the dream as a real event that demands explanation.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying: Apart from me — God will answer the welfare of Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Joseph answered Pharaoh, and his voice did not rise to meet the grandeur of the room. 'Not I,' he said. 'Apart from me. It is God who will answer — God, and the answer will be for the peace of Pharaoh.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph has just been told that he is credited with a gift: Pharaoh says he can 'hear a dream and open it'. His first word refuses the credit. Before a king who in Egyptian theology was himself a god, a prisoner says the answer belongs to another. Play it without false modesty and without defiance: it is a plain statement of where the power lies, spoken by a man who stands to gain everything if he takes the credit.

The Hebrew keeps a root that English scatters. 'Joseph answered' (vaya'an) and 'God will answer' (ya'aneh) come from the same verb, so Joseph's answer is a handing-over of the answering. Rashi and Radak read the second verb as God putting the answer into Joseph's mouth (Rashi: 'he will give an answer in my mouth'; Radak compares Prov 16:1, 'from the LORD is the answer of the tongue'). Ibn Ezra reads it differently, as 'will provide' — God will keep furnishing it — and compares Eccl 5:19, 'God provides (ma'aneh) him with joy of heart'. My own suggestion, not a classical reading: shalom is also the ordinary word for a greeting, so 'answer the shalom of Pharaoh' can echo a king's salutation being returned. The same word means welfare, so the sense is also 'God will answer for Pharaoh's well-being'.

The KJV 'It is not in me' is a paraphrase; the Hebrew is the blunter bil'adai, 'apart from me'. 'An answer of peace' turns the object (et shalom, the welfare of) into a modifier. Sforno takes the dreams to follow the mouth that interprets them (Berakhot 55b), which is why a good answer matters.

philological_notes.note: A compound 'apart from, without', here with the suffix 'me'. Ibn Ezra explains it as one word made of two (bal + 'ad). Not 'it is not in me' as in the KJV, but 'apart from me'.
'Will answer'. Rashi and Radak: God puts the answer in his mouth; Ibn Ezra: God will provide it, as in Eccl 5:19. It repeats the verb of 'and he answered'.
Welfare, wholeness, peace; also a greeting. That 'answering a greeting' hears here is my own suggestion.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph: In my dream, behold me, standing on the lip of the River.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Pharaoh spoke to Joseph. 'In my dream,' he said, 'I was standing — there, on the edge of the River.'
verses.directors_commentary:
Pharaoh now retells what the narrator told in verses 1–7, and he does not tell it the same way. Radak notes that when a man repeats a thing he adds, drops or changes words so long as the matter stays one; hear in this a king whose memory has been worrying at the dream for days. The first telling was seen from outside; this is first person and present: hinneni omed, 'behold me, standing'. Let the actor be there.

The River is ha-ye'or, a word of Egyptian origin (itrw) used almost only of the Nile and its channels, though Daniel 12:5–7 uses it of the Tigris, as Ramban notes on 41:1. For Pharaoh the Nile was the source of all life and of his own legitimacy; to see something rise out of it is to see something rise from the root of his kingdom. 'Lip of the river' is the Hebrew image for the bank, and the KJV 'bank' and 'I stood' lose the present participle: he is still standing, in the dream, as he speaks.

philological_notes.note: 'Behold, I': hinneh with the suffix 'I', followed by a participle, which makes the dream present. STEPBible 'if [was] I' is corrected here.
The River, an Egyptian loanword, used almost only of the Nile and its channels, but of the Tigris in Dan 12:5–7, as Ramban notes.

verses.translation_literal: And behold, from the Nile coming up, seven cows, fat of flesh and beautiful of form, and they grazed in the reed-grass.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, out of the river they rose, seven cows, sleek and heavy with flesh, lovely to look at. They moved into the reeds and began to graze.
verses.directors_commentary: Cows rising from water would strike an Egyptian as sacred. Hathor appears as a cow, and the river, the source of all fertility, is the cows' home. So these animals are no ordinary herd; they are the picture of abundance as the Egyptians themselves painted it. The Hebrew says 'fat of flesh' (bri'ot basar) and 'beautiful of form' (yefot to'ar), and the KJV's 'kine' and 'fatfleshed' are archaisms for the plain Hebrew words 'cows' and 'fat'. The last word, 'achu', is another Egyptian loan for reed-grass or marsh vegetation. The KJV's 'meadow' makes it sound dry. It is the green edge of the river, wet grass among the reeds. Onkelos keeps the foreign word as ba'achava.

philological_notes.note: 'In the reed-grass'. An Egyptian loan (akhu) for marsh vegetation by the Nile; the KJV's 'meadow' misses its wet setting. Onkelos preserves it as an Aramaic word.

verses.translation_literal: And behold, seven other cows coming up after them, weak and very bad of form and thin of flesh; I have not seen the like of them in all the land of Egypt for badness.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, behind them, seven others came up, hollow and wretched, nothing but hide stretched over bone, so foul to look at that I tell you, I have seen nothing like them in all the land of Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary: Now Pharaoh's voice cracks: this verse is where his version outruns the narrator's. The line 'I have not seen the like of them in all the land of Egypt for badness' is not in the account in 41:1-7; it is the king speaking, the man who has seen every herd in Egypt. The Hebrew builds the contrast out of sounds: bri'ot basar against raqqot basar, with the same word 'flesh' in both. Dallot (weak, hollow) is a word for the poor and the emaciated, and the KJV's 'poor' gives a social meaning, not the bodily one. Rashi ties it to Amnon's 'why are you so haggard?' (2 Sam 13:4) and glosses raqqot as 'lacking flesh'. Radak derives raqqot from raqaq, 'thin', as in the thin wafers of Exod 29:2. 'For badness' (lara') is a flat, bitter closing, and the KJV's 'for badness' is its literal match.

philological_notes.note: 'Weak', 'gaunt'. The KJV's 'poor' wrongly suggests poverty. Rashi compares Amnon's wasted look in 2 Samuel 13:4.
'Thin of flesh'. Rashi: wherever raqqot occurs it means 'lacking flesh'. Radak derives it from the thin wafers (rekikei) of Exod 29:2.

verses.translation_literal: And the cows ate, the thin ones and the bad ones, the seven cows, the first, the fat ones.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the gaunt, ugly cows turned on the others and ate them, the seven first cows, the fat ones, the lovely ones.
verses.directors_commentary: The horror is the plainness. Cows do not eat flesh, and the Hebrew uses the ordinary verb 'to eat', not a word of violence. The KJV's 'did eat up' adds an 'up' the Hebrew does not say. Say the line flatly: that is what makes it wrong. The word order repeats the earlier descriptions as if the king's mind were circling: the thin and the bad (haraqqot vehara'ot) eat the first, the fat. Radak points back to 'thin of flesh' in v. 19. The effect is a reversal of Egyptian symbols: the fertile cows of the Nile are consumed by famine.

verses.translation_literal: And they went into their inward parts, and it was not known that they had gone into their inward parts, and their appearance [was] bad as at the beginning. And I awoke.
verses.translation_dramatic: They went down into the thin cows' bellies, and nothing showed that they had gone in. The lean ones looked as bad as they had at first. And I woke.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the cruellest detail of the dream and the one the king cannot let go: the good has disappeared and left no trace. Pharaoh says it twice, almost word for word: 'they went into their inward parts, and it was not known that they had gone into their inward parts.' The repetition is the horror, as if the sentence itself kept swallowing. The KJV rewrites it as 'when they had eaten them up, it could not be known that they had eaten them', harmonizing it with verse 20 and adding an 'eaten' that is not in this verse; the Hebrew has only 'came into'. It then adds 'still' and 'So I awoke': the text has 'as at the beginning' and a bare 'and I awoke'.

Rashbam hears Pharaoh remembering aloud: the narrator could not have written this, since it was only what Pharaoh thought at the moment of the dream. Radak sees it prepared for Joseph's later words, 'and the plenty will not be known in the land' (41:31). Sforno compares the curse of Lev 26:26, 'you shall eat and not be satisfied', and the saying that a man with bread in his basket is not like a man with none (Yoma 74b): the famine is not only lack but food that does nothing. Ibn Ezra reads 'their appearance' as the appearance of each of the thin cows.

philological_notes.note: 'Their inward part': the innards, the belly. It is the word for the inside of a body, repeated twice; it is more physical than the English 'midst'.
'Was known': the passive. Radak links it to Joseph's 'and the plenty will not be known' (41:31).

verses.translation_literal: And I saw in my dream, and behold, seven ears of grain coming up on one stalk, full and good.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then I saw again, still within my dream: seven ears of grain, rising on a single stalk, heavy and good.
verses.directors_commentary: In the Hebrew the second dream follows in the same breath, 'and I saw in my dream', as one continuous experience. The KJV keeps it as one, and Sforno notes that Pharaoh knew from this that both visions were a single dream, while the diviners took them for two (see v. 24). Seven ears on one stalk is odd and slightly unnatural, as the dream should be, though emmer wheat and some Egyptian grains do bear several ears. 'Full and good' (mele'ot vetovot) echoes the first dream's 'fat and good-looking': abundance is a matter of weight and a matter of looks. The KJV's 'in one stalk' is fine.

philological_notes.note: 'Ears of grain'. Singular shibbolet, later the password in Judges 12.

verses.translation_literal: And behold, seven ears of grain, withered, thin, scorched by the east wind, sprouting after them.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then seven more, brittle and shrunken, seared by the east wind, pushing up behind them.
verses.directors_commentary: The second set is built from three words of loss: tzenumot, daqqot, shedufot qadim. The first is a hapax, a word found nowhere else in the Bible, and the commentators cannot agree on it: Rashi takes the Aramaic tzunma, hard as rock; Ramban rejects this and says 'broken into pieces' with gaps where the grain should be; Ibn Ezra says it has no parallel and means roughly 'empty'. The KJV 'withered' is a safe guess. 'Qadim' is the east wind that blows off the desert, and for an Egyptian the east and the desert belong to chaos and the god Seth, so this wind is not weather but an enemy. The KJV's 'blasted' is a good old word for it, and 'sprung up' is accurate. A modern reader might picture a hot, dry gust of the khamsin, which burns standing crops in a day.

philological_notes.note: A hapax of uncertain meaning: hard like rock (Rashi, from Aramaic tzunma), cut into pieces with gaps (Ramban), or simply empty (Ibn Ezra). 'Withered' is a conventional rendering, not a certainty.
The east wind, the hot desert wind that scorches crops (compare Hos 13:15).

verses.translation_literal: And the thin ears swallowed the seven good ears. And I said to the diviner-priests, and there was no one telling me.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the thin ears swallowed the seven good ones whole. I told it to my wise men, the sacred scribes of the house of life, and not one of them could tell me what it meant.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the verb is stronger than in v. 20: 'swallowed' (bala'), not 'ate'. The thin grain does to the good what the thin cows did to the fat. Then the wall: 'I said to the hartummim, and there was none to tell me.' These are the Egyptian ritual experts, the 'chief lector priests', the keepers of the sacred texts and the interpreters of omens, and their failure is the point; the KJV's 'magicians' is a Hebrew-flavoured guess and the BBE's 'wise men' is vaguer still. Sforno notes that they probably failed because they took the dreams as two separate ones and gave two separate readings, where Pharaoh knew they were one. 'And there was none telling me' ends in two small syllables, li, 'to me': the king of Egypt left alone with his own dream. That is the silence into which Joseph's answer will fall.

philological_notes.note: Egyptian court experts in sacred writing and magic, probably from Egyptian ḥry-tp, 'chief (lector priest)'. Onkelos renders 'sorcerers' (חרשיא).
'One who tells' or 'declares'. Sforno reads the failure as the diviners treating one dream as two.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph said to Pharaoh: The dream of Pharaoh, one it [is]. [That] which God [is] about to do, he has told to Pharaoh.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph answered Pharaoh, and his voice did not tremble. "The dream of Pharaoh is one dream. One. What God is about to do, he has told to Pharaoh."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph opens by taking the sting out of the moment: the court's experts have failed because they treated two dreams as two riddles. He says it is one dream, and his first act is to give the credit to God, not to himself. Before a king who is himself a god, that is a bold sentence, and it is polite only because it puts Pharaoh at the centre: God has told *Pharaoh*, and Joseph is only the reader.

The KJV's "God hath shewed Pharaoh what he is about to do" is fair, but "shewed" blurs the distinction the Hebrew draws: here the verb is *higgid*, "told, declared", and in verse 28 it is *her'ah*, "made to see". The participle "is about to do" (*oseh*) means that the action is already under way. Sforno takes the point that the magicians went wrong because they did not know this was one dream.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of *n-g-d*, "to declare, make plain". Here it is spoken communication; in verse 28 the verb changes to "made to see". Rashi on 41:26 takes the two verbs as marking near events (told) against distant ones (shown).
"It is one": the two dreams, the cows and the ears, are a single message. Sforno says this is why the interpreters erred.

verses.translation_literal: The seven cows, the good: seven years they. And the seven ears, the good: seven years they. One dream it.
verses.translation_dramatic: The seven good cows — they are seven years. The seven good ears — they, too, are seven years. It is one dream.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph interprets without a pause or a flourish. The Hebrew has no 'are'; it sets the images and their meanings side by side: 'seven cows, the good — seven years, they.' Keep it hammered and plain. A man who was in prison until yesterday is now the only person in the room who is certain.

The verse says the same thing twice and then names it as one: 'one dream it.' Rashi reads the fourteen as in fact only seven, and the dream was doubled because the matter is prepared (mezumman), settled by God; and he links the doubling to the verb choices elsewhere: of the good years Joseph says higgid, 'he told', because they are near, while the distant famine is something God 'has caused to be seen' (hereah). So the pairing is not redundancy but a seal. The KJV 'kine' is archaic for us, though it was not in 1611, when it was the ordinary plural; the Hebrew parot is simply 'cows'. The English also loses the plain rhythm: the Hebrew has no 'are', and the KJV supplies it.

Note that Pharaoh's cows were 'fat of flesh' (41:18), while Joseph calls them 'the good': he moves from description to meaning.

philological_notes.note: The feminine plural 'they', the whole copula: 'seven years they'. There is no verb 'to be'.
'One dream it.' Rashi: the fourteen are only seven, and the dream is doubled because the matter is prepared (mezumman); 'near' explains higgid.

verses.translation_literal: And the seven cows, the thin and the bad, the ones coming up after them — seven years they. And the seven ears, the empty, scorched of the east wind, they will be seven years of famine.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the seven lean, ugly cows that came up after them — they are seven years. And the seven empty ears, scorched by the east wind — they will be seven years of famine.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the mood turns, and the shift is in a single word: until now everything has been 'are'; the ears 'will be' (yihyu), and only now is the word famine (ra'av) said aloud. Let the room go cold on it. Ramban explains the order: plenty in Egypt is no novelty, since the land is like the garden of the LORD (Gen 13:10), so the interpretation begins with the bad years, which are the news and the point of the dream; God showed Pharaoh the famine in mercy, so that a great remnant might live. He adds that the famine's coming is not known before the famine years themselves.

Joseph also changes Pharaoh's words. Pharaoh's ears were 'thin' (daqqot, 41:23); Joseph says 'empty' (rekot). Ramban on 41:23 thinks this is deliberate and exact. The sound is close to that of the cows, haraqqot, 'the thin', against hareqot, 'the empty': Radak derives the first from raqaq and the second from the root of 'the pit was empty' (Gen 37:24), the same word used of the pit where Joseph himself was thrown. A listener hears the two as near-twins. My own observation, not a classical one: ra'ot, 'bad', and ra'av, 'famine', are a near-echo, not the same word, and the ear catches that closeness.

The KJV 'blasted' for shedufot softens a drying wind that scorches; 'kine' is only an old plural, not a mistake. The cows 'that came up after them' keeps the participle of 41:23.

philological_notes.note: 'The empty'. Radak derives it from the 'empty' of the pit in Gen 37:24, and the thin cows' haraqqot from raqaq. Joseph replaces Pharaoh's 'thin' (daqqot) with 'empty'.
Famine, hunger. It sounds close to ra'ot ('bad') without being the same word; that near-echo is my own observation.

verses.translation_literal: It [is] the word which I spoke to Pharaoh: [that] which God [is] about to do, he has made Pharaoh see.
verses.translation_dramatic: "This is the word I spoke to you, my lord: what God is about to do, he has let Pharaoh see."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph closes the first half of his speech by returning to its first claim, almost word for word: a rhetorician's ring. It tells Pharaoh that nothing has been added or hidden: what Joseph says is what the dream says.

Now the verb changes from "told" (v. 25) to "made to see" (*her'ah*). Radak points out the two verbs are a deliberate pair, and Sforno ties "seeing" to the years of plenty, which show the king how to save his people. The KJV's present tense, "he sheweth", flattens the perfect: the showing has already happened, in the night.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil, "he caused to see". The verb pairs with *higgid* of v. 25; Radak notes the pairing with 1 Sam 3:15.

verses.translation_literal: Behold: seven years coming, great plenty in all the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Look. Seven years are coming, years of great plenty, over every field of the land of Egypt."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph begins with the good news. *Hinneh*, "behold", is a spoken pointing finger, the same word that opened Pharaoh's dream report. Egypt in a good year was the granary of the ancient Near East, so plenty is not the surprise; but "in all the land of Egypt" marks the whole country, from Delta to cataracts, as sharing in it.

The KJV "plenty" is right. The word *sava'* is a noun, "satiety, abundance" (Ibn Ezra insists that it is a noun, as *ra'av* "famine" is, not a verb).

philological_notes.note: "Plenty, satiety", a noun parallel to *ra'av* "famine". Ibn Ezra stresses that it is a noun, not a verb form.

verses.translation_literal: And they will arise, seven years of famine after them; and all the plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt; and the famine will finish off the land.
verses.translation_dramatic: "Then, behind them, seven years of famine will stand up. And all that plenty will be forgotten in the land of Egypt, forgotten as though it had never been, and the famine will eat the land to its end."
verses.directors_commentary:
Three verbs, one after the other, and each one is a step downward: the famine *rises* (it stands up like an army), the plenty is *forgotten*, and the land is *finished*. The verb *kalah* means "to bring to an end" and is the one used of an enemy's total destruction; "consume" in the KJV is a good old word, but it makes the famine sound like a mouth, where Hebrew makes it a verdict.

The forgetting is the psychological horror: in a famine nobody remembers what a full belly was. Rashi reads this as the interpretation of the thin cows swallowing the fat ones without a trace (v. 21), and Rashbam compares it to "it was not known that they had come into their bellies".

philological_notes.note: Niphal, "it will be forgotten". Rashi: the interpretation of the swallowing, since memory of plenty is swallowed too.
Piel of *k-l-h*, "to finish, to bring to an end, to destroy". Onkelos softens the object to the people of the land.

verses.translation_literal: And the plenty will not be known in the land because of that famine after thus, for heavy it [is], very.
verses.translation_dramatic: "No one will be able to say that there was ever plenty in the land. The famine that follows will be too heavy, far too heavy, for anyone to remember."
verses.directors_commentary:
The Hebrew "will not be known" is stronger than a failure of memory: the plenty will not be recognizable, as the swallowed cows left no trace of having eaten (Rashi, Ibn Ezra). The KJV "grievous" is a Latinate choice that hides the physical word *kaved*, "heavy". In Hebrew, famine is a weight on the land, and the same root describes Pharaoh's hardened heart in Exodus.

The repetition "that famine" (*ha-ra'av ha-hu*) points at it as if it were already in the room.

philological_notes.note: "Heavy", used of weight, burden and severity. The KJV "grievous" is figurative; the Hebrew is concrete.

verses.translation_literal: And concerning the repeating of the dream to Pharaoh two times: for the matter [is] fixed from with God, and God [is] hurrying to do it.
verses.translation_dramatic: "And as for the dream coming to Pharaoh twice, this is why: the matter is settled, settled with God, and God is already hurrying to do it."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph explains the one thing that must have troubled Pharaoh most: why twice? His answer is theological, not technical: a doubled dream is a doubled seal. In the ancient world, a repeated omen was a confirmed one, and Joseph says the confirmation comes from God, not from any magician's art.

The KJV's "doubled" and "shortly" are acceptable, but the Hebrew has two verbs worth keeping: "fixed" (*nakhon*, "established, prepared", Rashi: *mezumman*) and "hurrying" (*memaher*). The famine is not far away in the abstract; God is moving. Ramban adds that the odd thing was that both dreams came in one night, which is not how dreams go, and that is itself a sign of haste.

philological_notes.note: Niphal infinitive, "the being repeated", from *sh-n-h* "to repeat, double" (Ibn Ezra), a different root from *shanah* "year" despite the likeness.
"Fixed, established, ready". Rashi glosses it as appointed and prepared.

verses.translation_literal: And now let Pharaoh see a man discerning and wise, and let him set him over the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: So now, let Pharaoh look about him and find a man, a man with insight and with wisdom, and set that man over the whole land of Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pivot of the scene. Joseph has finished interpreting; he could have stopped, and the dream would still have been explained. Instead he turns advice into a job description, and the actor must decide how much Joseph knows he is describing himself. He never says 'me.' Ramban reads it as tactical: Joseph said all this so that they would choose him, "for the wise man's eyes are in his head" (Eccl 2:14), meaning that the wise see ahead and he sees where the conversation is going. Sforno hears something more devout: God has revealed both the famine and the plenty, so Pharaoh must now look for the right instrument.

The KJV says 'look out a man discreet and wise.' 'Look out' is old English for 'seek out'; the Hebrew is simply 'let Pharaoh see,' with the same verb as Pharaoh's dream, which gives the line its irony: the king who saw the cows must now see a man. 'Discreet' is archaic for 'discerning' (nabon, from the root for understanding and distinguishing). Sforno takes the pair as thinker and doer, 'theoretical and practical,' in running provinces. In the Egyptian setting, an official of this kind is a vizier in everything but name.

philological_notes.note: A niphal participle of the root 'to discern': one who can tell things apart and read what is coming. Paired with 'wise' (chakham) it names the double qualification Joseph is going to prove: insight into the future, and skill in managing the present.

'Let him see,' as the KJV's 'look out' shows, is a sense of selecting by inspection. The same verb opens the dream report earlier in the chapter, so the narrative sets Pharaoh's seeing on both sides of the interpretation.

verses.translation_literal: Let Pharaoh act, and let him appoint overseers over the land, and let him take a fifth of the land of Egypt in the seven years of the plenty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Let Pharaoh act. Let him set overseers over the land, and in the seven years of plenty let him take a fifth of Egypt's yield for himself.
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph is no longer interpreting; he is legislating, and he does it in a rhythm of short commands: act, appoint, take a fifth. A good Joseph is not breathless here. He is giving an administrator's briefing to a monarch.

The Hebrew, and the KJV after it, says 'the fifth part of the land of Egypt'; in context it means the land's produce, not the soil, and the BBE rightly says 'a fifth part of the produce.' The ambiguity is part of the trap for readers: no one is proposing to seize a fifth of the country. A fifth, one part in five, is a heavy but survivable tax, set against a harvest so large that, as the next verses say, no one will miss it.

The verb חִמֵּשׁ is rare and divides the commentators. Rashi follows Onkelos, 'and let him urge them on' or mobilize, and links it to 'armed' (chamushim) in Exodus 13:18; Radak, Ibn Ezra and Pseudo-Jonathan take it as 'take a fifth.' The second reading suits the sentence that follows, where the fifth is gathered and stored. Rashbam adds a parallel from 1 Samuel 8, where the king takes a tenth of the fields, and sees in Joseph's measure a harsher levy than usual. Sforno explains the overseers: appointed in every city so that they would be recognized as one body under a single authority and not be divided in opinion.

philological_notes.note: A denominative piel from 'five': 'take a fifth.' Rashi and Onkelos instead read 'organize' or 'urge on,' as in Ex 13:18; the traditional division is real, and I follow the tax reading because the fifth is what is gathered in the next verse.
'Overseers,' those who are put in charge by being 'visited' or mustered. Sforno says they were to be set up in every city so as to be recognized as officers of one purpose, not rivals.
