verses.translation_literal: And let them gather all the food of these good years that are coming, and let them store up grain under the hand of Pharaoh, food in the cities, and let them keep [it].
verses.translation_dramatic: Let them gather every scrap of the food of these good years that are coming, and heap up the grain under Pharaoh's own hand, food in the cities, and let them guard it.
verses.directors_commentary:
The plan is spelled out in verbs: gather, store, keep. All of them are in the third person plural, so the speaker never says who 'they' are; the overseers of the last verse are meant, and Joseph keeps himself out of the sentence. The tension is quiet: abundance, and one man saying that it must not be eaten.

The KJV's 'corn' is the English habit of calling grain, of whatever kind, 'corn,' and in Egypt it means wheat and barley; the Hebrew bar is cleaned grain. 'Under the hand of Pharaoh' is not a figure of speech for authority only: Rashi glosses it as in his control and his storehouses, and Rashbam hears the royal collection of Esther 2:3, where the king appoints officers to gather. Radak goes further and has storehouses of Pharaoh in every city, holding the fifth that Pharaoh takes, apart from whatever each person puts by for himself. The repeated 'food' shows a plan that is both a collection and a siting: the cities are the barns.

Ibn Ezra raises the practical worry that Egypt's air is damp from the Nile, so that grain could not last seven years unless it were mixed with something that preserves it, and Ramban cites the rabbis' reports of earth and sorts of preservatives for the same reason. This is why Joseph's wisdom is described as practical as well as visionary.

philological_notes.note: 'Food' as a noun, which Rashi distinguishes from the participle 'eating' (okhel) by its stress and vowel.
'Under the hand of Pharaoh': in his custody. Rashi reads it as in his authority and in his storehouses.

verses.translation_literal: And the food will become a deposit for the land, for the seven years of the famine which will be in the land of Egypt; and the land will not be cut off by the famine.
verses.translation_dramatic: "So the food will lie in store for the land, a deposit kept for the seven years of famine that will come upon Egypt. And the land will not be cut off by hunger."
verses.directors_commentary:
Joseph ends where the whole speech was heading: not profit, not a tax, but survival. The food is a *piqqadon*, a deposit, the word for goods placed in trust with someone to hold. The grain is, in effect, entrusted by the good years to the bad. The land is the beneficiary, and the verb at the end, *tikkaret*, "be cut off", is the one used of covenants and of whole peoples severed from their roots.

The KJV's "that the land perish not" turns the closing clause into a purpose, which is the sense, but loses the plain statement of the Hebrew, "and the land will not be cut off." Rashi: the stored grain is like any hidden deposit, kept for the land's survival. Radak: it will be found when needed.

philological_notes.note: "Deposit, entrusted goods", from *p-k-d*, and so a verbal echo of the "overseers" (*pekidim*) of v. 34. Rashi and Radak both read it as goods held in trust for later need.
Niphal of *k-r-t*, "to cut off". The same root as "cut a covenant".

verses.translation_literal: And the word was good in the eyes of Pharaoh, and in the eyes of all his servants.
verses.translation_dramatic: The words settled over the hall like cool water on a hot day. Pharaoh heard them and found them good; and in the same breath every servant who stood along the walls found them good as well.
verses.directors_commentary: Watch the room, not the speaker. In an Egyptian court the king's face is the weather, and 'good in the eyes of' is the formula for approval by a ruler; the servants' approval is listed second because it follows his. Play it as a collective exhale: Joseph has just told a god-king that the land will starve, and the court chooses to believe it. The Hebrew says 'the word' (hadavar), which means 'the matter' as well as 'the speech': they approve both the interpretation and the plan Joseph added to it. The KJV's 'the thing' is fair; BBE's 'seemed good' turns approval into an impression, which is weaker than the Hebrew. Radak notes why they trusted him: the interpretation fitted the dream so closely, the cupbearer had vouched for him, and Joseph spoke briefly and plainly.

philological_notes.note: 'Word' and 'thing/matter' in one noun. Here the speech and the proposal it carries are both approved.
'In the eyes of' is the standard idiom for a superior's judgment; it is repeated for Pharaoh and for his servants, so the approval is public and complete.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh said to his servants, Is one found like this, a man in whom is the spirit of God?
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Pharaoh turned to his servants. "Is there anyone to be found like this man," he said, "a man in whom the spirit of God lives?"
verses.directors_commentary:
Pharaoh does not ask Joseph; he asks the room. This is a court, and the king needs its assent before he puts a foreign prisoner over Egypt. The question is rhetorical, and the answer expected is no.

The verb is the hard part. 'Hanimtza' can be read as one word, a niphal 'is one found?', which is Ibn Ezra's first reading, and the sense of the KJV's 'can we find.' Ibn Ezra also allows that the opening nun is a sign of the speakers, 'shall we find,' and Rashi and Radak read it that way: 'if we go and look for him, will one like him be found?' The KJV and ASV's 'can we find' follows the plural. Ramban adds a social reason for the form: Joseph was a Hebrew, whom Egyptians held unclean, so Pharaoh first had to win his servants to the idea.

'Spirit of God' is Elohim. For a polytheist king this could as well be 'a divine spirit' or 'spirit of the gods'; the Hebrew narrator makes it the word that Joseph himself has used, so that the same name reaches Pharaoh's mouth. The Targum turns it into 'spirit of prophecy from before the LORD,' which is an interpretive gloss; Rashbam understands the spirit as a gift for interpreting dreams and, all the more, for the wisdom of statecraft.

philological_notes.note: The interrogative he plus a niphal 'is found' (Ibn Ezra's first reading). Ibn Ezra, with Rashi and Radak, also allows a first-person plural: 'shall we find?'
'The spirit of God' or 'of a god.' Onkelos renders it 'spirit of prophecy from before the LORD'; Rashbam says it covers dream interpretation and above all practical wisdom.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "After God has made known to you all this, there is no one discerning and wise like you."
verses.translation_dramatic: And now he turned to Joseph. "Since God has shown you all of this," said Pharaoh, "there is no one as understanding, no one as wise, as you."
verses.directors_commentary: The king shifts from the third person to 'you'. This is the moment of address, and it is also a legal reason: Pharaoh gives a ground for the appointment ('after God has made known...') before he gives the office. The reason is Joseph's own claim from verses 16 and 25-28, now adopted by the king. The KJV's 'forasmuch as' is a stiff way to say 'after', and 'discreet' is now a word about keeping secrets; the Hebrew navon means 'discerning', someone who can tell things apart and see what will follow. Rashbam splits the pair: the discerning one understands the future, the wise one has gathered knowledge from what he has seen and heard. The two adjectives are the very qualities Joseph said Pharaoh should look for in verse 33 ('a man discerning and wise'); Pharaoh now says that the man has been found and it is the one who described him. That is the irony: Joseph advertised a job and Pharaoh found the applicant in the room.

philological_notes.note: 'Discerning and wise'. The same pair Joseph named in verse 33 as the qualities needed for the overseer. Rashbam reads navon as foresight and chakham as accumulated learning.

verses.translation_literal: You, you shall be over my house, and upon your mouth shall all my people kiss; only the throne shall I be greater than you.
verses.translation_dramatic: You will stand over my house. At your word, all my people will bow and kiss the ground, and to the throne alone will I be higher than you.
verses.directors_commentary:
Pharaoh gives with one hand and marks the boundary with the other: you, over my house; all my people on your word; only the throne above you. The actor should play the final clause with a king's calm, as a reminder that he is the one who gives.

The KJV's 'according unto thy word shall all my people be ruled' is a paraphrase, and it loses the Hebrew's image, 'upon your mouth shall all my people kiss.' The verb yishaq is from the root for 'kiss' (nashaq); I translate it so, as homage and obedience to the one who speaks. The commentators did not agree. Rashi reads it as 'be provisioned': all that my people need will be done by your hand, and cites Psalm 2:12 ('nashqu bar'); Onkelos renders it 'be sustained.' Rashbam and Radak relate it to nesheq, 'weapon,' and Ibn Ezra, who reads the doubled shin as a dropped nun, says the sense is 'a commander of the host,' and mentions 'some say' the kiss derivation but judges it far-fetched.

'Only the throne' (hakisse) is, for Rashi, the royal title: 'only that they will call me king.' Radak: 'in the matter of the throne I will be greater.' Ibn Ezra stresses that the verb is intransitive: no greatness greater than yours, except the greatness of the throne. Nothing in the verse names a vizier's office, but the 'house' is the royal household and, by extension, the state.

philological_notes.note: From 'kiss': the people will do homage upon his mouth. This is my own literal choice. Rashi reads 'be provisioned' (cf. Ps 2:12), Onkelos 'be sustained,' and Rashbam, Radak and Ibn Ezra derive it from nesheq 'weapon' (Ibn Ezra: 'commander'). Ibn Ezra calls the kissing derivation far-fetched.
'The throne,' standing for the kingship. Rashi: only that they will call me king; Radak: in the matter of the throne.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, "See, I have set you over all the land of Egypt."
verses.translation_dramatic: Pharaoh said to Joseph, "Look. I have set you over the whole land of Egypt."
verses.directors_commentary: A short line, a formal one. 'See' (re'eh) is the herald's word that opens a decree, and the perfect 'I have set' (natati) is a performative: by saying it Pharaoh does it. Rashbam hears it spoken as the ring changes hands in the next verse. Sforno reads 'see' as a warning, look well to what you have been given, and Radak as an order to govern by Joseph's own judgment. Play it low and plain; the decree needs no ornament. 'Set' is also a pun on the verb natan, 'give': the same verb will return in verse 43 and 45, as Pharaoh gives Joseph the office and the bride. Rashi observes that natan is used for both promotion and humiliation. The KJV and ASV are accurate here; the only gap is that English 'see' has lost its force as a call to attention.

philological_notes.note: 'I give / I set'. The perfect is performative: it enacts the appointment as it is spoken. Rashi notes that natan can be used of raising or lowering.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh removed his signet-ring from upon his hand, and he set it on the hand of Joseph, and he clothed him [in] garments of fine linen, and he put the chain of gold on his neck.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Pharaoh drew the signet from his own hand and pressed it onto Joseph's. He had him robed in fine linen, white and soft as light; and around Joseph's neck he laid a chain of gold.
verses.directors_commentary: Four gestures, each handed over in turn, and each is a legal act, not decoration. The ring is the seal: whatever Joseph presses it into becomes the king's own order, which is why Ramban cites Esther 8:8 ('seal it with the king's ring'). The Hebrew has Pharaoh remove it 'from upon his hand' and put it 'on the hand of Joseph', so the hand that held the power is bare for a moment. Next comes the clothing: Joseph, who has been stripped of his coat twice (the striped robe, then the cloak left in Potiphar's wife's grasp) and has worn a prisoner's rags, is now dressed by a king. The 'fine linen' (shesh) is Egyptian linen woven so thin that it is nearly transparent; Rashi and Rashbam call it prized in Egypt. The KJV's 'vestures' is old-fashioned for 'garments', but accurate. The gold collar (ravid) is the Egyptian 'gold of honour', given by the king to his favourites; the word occurs only here and in Ezekiel 16:11, so the English 'chain' is a best guess, and Rashi derives it from rows of links. Stage it slowly; each object should land.

philological_notes.note: 'His signet-ring', an instrument of authority that seals documents. Rashi: giving it marks the recipient as second to the king. Ramban prefers the plain sense: the seal itself, to command in the king's name.
Fine white linen, an Egyptian specialty and marker of status.
A rare word for a necklace or collar, from a root meaning 'to spread'. Rashi connects it with rows of rings and with Proverbs 7:16 ('I have spread my bed'). Only here and Ezekiel 16:11.

verses.translation_literal: And he made him ride in the chariot of the second which was his, and they called out before him, Avrekh! and putting him over all the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: He had him ride in the chariot that came second to his own, and the cry went up before him: Avrekh! Thus Joseph was set over the whole land of Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the king's words become a procession. The chariot carries the scene; the single cry before it is the sound of it. The Hebrew has one word, 'Avrekh,' and no runners, and nothing says how many voices called it. The people are told, in public, who the man is.

Nobody is certain what 'avrekh' means, and the commentators say so. The KJV's 'bow the knee' is a good guess and the oldest: Sforno takes it as an imperative like 'hav'rekh,' 'kneel!', a cry telling the people to bend the knee before him. Ibn Ezra reads it with a first-person aleph, 'I will kneel' (his own view), the way each person calls out as the chariot passes, and reports R. Yonah the Spanish grammarian, who takes it as an infinitive, 'to kneel,' with the aleph standing for a he; Radak adds that it is an infinitive like the 'natun' that ends the verse. The Targum Onkelos reads it as Aramaic, 'this is the father (abba) of the king,' which Rashi cites; Rashbam explains it as a father to the king, an official serving the king's needs. Rashi also reports the midrash 'father in wisdom and tender in years,' which R. Yose ben Durmaskit rejects as twisting the text: it is a word of knees.

The chariot is 'of the mishneh,' the second. Rashi and Ramban's first reading: the one that goes next to the king's own. Ramban prefers 'the viceroy's chariot,' since mishneh is an adjective for second in rank, as in 1 Samuel 23:17 and Esther 10:3. The KJV's 'second chariot' reads the first way. The last clause is an infinitive absolute with no subject, 'and putting him,' which the KJV and ASV smooth into a finite verb, 'he made him ruler.'

philological_notes.note: A rare, unexplained word, most likely linked to 'knee' (berekh). Sforno: imperative 'kneel,' like hav'rekh. Ibn Ezra: first-person 'I will kneel' (his own preference), and R. Yonah as infinitive. Onkelos reads 'this is father of the king,' which Rashi cites and Rashbam explains; Rashi also reports a midrash that R. Yose ben Durmaskit rejects.
'The second,' either the chariot second to the king's or the chariot of the second in rank. Ramban prefers an adjective for rank, as in 1 Sam 23:17 and Est 10:3.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh said to Joseph, I am Pharaoh, and apart from you no man shall lift up his hand and his foot in all the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Pharaoh spoke to Joseph, and the words were simple. "I am Pharaoh. Without you, no man in all the land of Egypt shall lift a hand or a foot."
verses.directors_commentary:
The ceremony is done and the king says it plainly: 'I am Pharaoh.' It is a statement of who holds the power before he gives it away. Then the gift: without you, no one lifts a hand or foot. The man who receives it is a man who was in prison this morning: Genesis 41:14 has him hurried out of the pit, and the text gives no clock beyond that scene, so the actor can let the whiplash show.

The KJV's 'I am Pharaoh, and without thee shall no man lift up his hand or foot' is close, apart from 'or' for the Hebrew 'and.' The commentators read the first clause as the grounds for the second. Rashi reads it as 'I have power in my hand to decree for my kingdom, and I decree that no one lift a hand without your leave'; he adds an alternative, 'I am Pharaoh, I will be king,' which he says is the same as 'only the throne' in verse 40. Rashbam gives that link too: 'I am king, and this is the 'only the throne am I greater than you.'' Radak: even though I am king, without your permission no one will lift his hand or foot for any matter. Ibn Ezra takes 'foot' as the right to walk, or as a figure.

Onkelos is more concrete: no one may lift a hand to take up arms or a foot to ride a horse; Rashbam finds 'lifting a hand' in the story of Jeroboam in 1 Kings 11, who lifted his hand against the king under Solomon's appointment. In both, the phrase means to act with authority.

philological_notes.note: 'No man shall lift up hand and foot': no one shall act. Onkelos makes it concrete (to take up arms, to ride a horse); Ibn Ezra reads foot as the right to go, or as a figure; Rashbam compares Jeroboam 'who lifted up a hand against the king' (1 Kgs 11:26).
A verbless sentence, 'I am Pharaoh.' Rashi: I have power in my hand to decree on my kingdom; or: I am the king, as in 'only the throne.' Rashbam links it to verse 40 in the same way.

verses.translation_literal: And Pharaoh called the name of Joseph Zaphenath-paneah, and he gave him Asenath, daughter of Poti-phera, priest of On, as a wife; and Joseph went out over the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Pharaoh gave Joseph a new name, an Egyptian one: Zaphenath-paneah. And he gave him a wife, Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On. Then Joseph went out, a lord over the land of Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary: Joseph is re-made in three steps: a name, a wife, a mission. Every ancient court renamed the men it adopted: compare Daniel, renamed Belteshazzar (Rashbam, Radak). The new name is Egyptian; Radak says it is wrong to look for it in Hebrew, and Ibn Ezra admits it cannot be translated, while Rashi, followed by the Targums, takes it to mean 'revealer of secrets'. A common modern proposal (my own reading, unsourced) is an Egyptian phrase like 'God speaks and he lives', which would suit a man who just saved Pharaoh's land. The wife is the daughter of a priest of On, the sun-city of Re (later Greek Heliopolis), the oldest cult centre in the country, so Joseph is married into the top of the religious order, which would have mattered more to Egyptians than the name. The name Asenath probably means 'she belongs to Neith' (own reading) and Potiphera 'the one whom Ra gave'. Rashi's midrash that Potiphera is Potiphar, renamed after his castration, is a rabbinic story reaching across chapters, not a reading of this verse, and Rashbam says plainly that on the plain sense they are not the same man. The KJV 'went out over' stays close to the Hebrew, as the verb 'went out' is also military and ceremonial, and Ibn Ezra reads it as his name going out. The BBE's 'went through' flattens the verb. Play 'went out over' as a king stepping out of his palace.

philological_notes.note: Egyptian name of uncertain meaning. Rashi gives 'revealer of hidden things' and the Targums follow; Ibn Ezra says if it is Egyptian we do not know the meaning and if translated it does not match 'Joseph'; Radak insists it is Egyptian, as Daniel's new name was Aramaic/Babylonian. A proposed Egyptian sense, 'God speaks and he lives', is my own reading.

'Priest of On'. Ramban and Ibn Ezra debate whether kohen here means a priest of a god or a high official; Rashbam says a ruler of the city, citing 'David's sons were kohanim'. On is the city of the sun-god, later Heliopolis.
'He went out': to take up his charge (Radak), in a manner that showed him ruler (Sforno), or his fame went out (Ibn Ezra).

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph [was] a son of thirty years when he stood before Pharaoh, king of Egypt; and Joseph went out from before Pharaoh, and he passed through all the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: Joseph was thirty years old on the day he stood before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. He went out from Pharaoh's presence, and he passed through the whole of the land.
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator steps back and does the arithmetic. Joseph was seventeen when his brothers sold him (Genesis 37:2), so thirteen years lie between the pit and this palace, most of them in a slave's quarters and a prison cell. Thirty is also the age of full standing in the ancient world; Rashbam says he was old enough for rule. 'Stood before' is the language of service: a courtier stands before the king, and the verse closes the loop by having him 'go out from before' him, from servant to governor. The KJV 'went throughout' is correct, but the verb is 'passed through', a tour of inspection: Radak says he went to survey the realm's affairs, and Sforno compares Samuel's circuit in 1 Samuel 7:16. Play it as a man learning the size of what he now owns.

philological_notes.note: 'Son of thirty years' is the Hebrew idiom for age. Rashbam adds that thirty is the age fit for rule.
'He passed through': an inspection circuit. Radak says it was to inspect royal affairs; Sforno to visit cities and set them in order, like Samuel's circuit in 1 Samuel 7:16.

verses.translation_literal: And the land made, in the seven years of the plenty, to handfuls.
verses.translation_dramatic: And in the seven years of plenty the land did more than give; it gave by the handful, fist after fist of grain, as though the earth could not open its hand without spilling.
verses.directors_commentary: Hebrew says the land 'made' ('asah), and the KJV's 'brought forth' is an idiomatic rendering of that verb as Rashbam reads it: the land produced a great deal of grain, as in 'and it shall make the produce for the three years' (Lev 25:21), which Rashbam cites. Rashi, by contrast, says the verb does not leave the sense of making. The oddest word is liqmatzim, 'to handfuls', a plural of qomets, the closed-fist scoop of a reaper or a priest measuring flour. The KJV, ASV and Webster keep 'by handfuls'; the BBE's 'in masses' loses the picture of a hand. The Hebrew can be heard two ways: Rashbam and Sforno hear the crop itself (a single stalk or ear full of handfuls), Rashi that they stored it 'handful on handful, hand on hand'. Play it so that either can be felt: abundance so ordinary that nobody counts in anything larger than a fist. Ramban adds that Onkelos has 'to storehouses' (le'otsarin), reading qematzim as pits dug for storage.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'made'. Rashbam takes it as 'produced much grain', comparing Lev 25:21; the KJV's 'brought forth' is that idiomatic sense. Rashi says the word does not depart from the sense of making.

'By handfuls': qomets is a fistful. Rashi hears 'handful on handful they stored'; Rashbam 'a full handful of ears on one stalk'; Radak 'many handfuls from a single grain'; Sforno 'handfuls in every ear'.

verses.translation_literal: And he gathered [obj] all the food of seven years which were in the land of Egypt, and he put food in the cities; the food of the field of the city which [was] around it, he put in its midst.
verses.translation_dramatic: He gathered up the food of all those seven years in the land of Egypt, and he set it down in the cities. The grain of the fields that ringed each town he brought in and laid within its own walls.
verses.directors_commentary: This is logistics as theology: the plan of the dreams becomes a supply chain. The Hebrew word 'okhel, 'food', appears three times in the verse, flat and repeated like an inventory; the KJV keeps 'food' each time but smooths the rhythm, while the BBE swaps in 'produce' and names Joseph, which the Hebrew does not. The KJV's 'every city' also adds a word: the Hebrew has 'the city', singular and distributive, meaning each town in turn, and 'in the same' is its 'in its midst'. The logic is local. Each city stores the yield of its own surrounding fields, so no grain has to travel far, and Rashi adds that each region's grain was kept with the soil of the place, which preserved it from rot. Radak notes that the storehouses were in cities, not villages. Ibn Ezra takes 'all' as 'all he could'; Ramban prefers all of it, gathered under Pharaoh's hand with a ration given out yearly.

philological_notes.note: 'All the food'. Ibn Ezra says 'all' cannot be literal, as the people would have starved; he means all that he could gather. Ramban argues it was literally everything edible, held under Pharaoh's hand.
'The food of the field of the city', the produce of the countryside around each town, put inside the town it surrounds. Rashi: every region kept its own produce, with the soil of the place.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph stored up grain like the sand of the sea, much, exceedingly, until he ceased to count, for there was no count.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Joseph heaped up grain like the sand of the sea, so much, so very much, that at last he stopped counting, for there was no count to be kept.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse ends on a hammered root: lispor, 'to count', and mispar, 'a count'. The KJV and ASV keep the repetition ('numbering... without number'), though 'left numbering' sounds dated; the BBE changes 'number' to 'measure' but also keeps the repetition ('measuring... measured'). STEPBible glosses lisPor as 'to measure', which is not the root: sapar is counting, unlike the verb shavar 'to deal in grain' in 41:56-57. 'Corn' in the KJV is the old English word for any grain; bar is wheat or cleaned grain. 'Like the sand of the sea' is conventional hyperbole (Radak: derekh haflagah). Give it the weight of awe rather than a figure: the official whose job was to count has reached the end of what counting can do. Rashi reads the verse as terse: the counter stopped counting, and 'for' means 'because'. The phrase also echoes the sand-of-the-sea language used for numerous descendants (Gen 32:13); that echo is one reading you may or may not want to play.

philological_notes.note: 'To count'. It repeats in mispar, 'a count', and the pair is the verse's closing wordplay; STEPBible's 'to measure' is corrected here.
'Until he ceased': Rashi supplies a subject, the counter, and calls the verse short or elliptical. Radak says 'like the sand of the sea' is exaggeration.

verses.translation_literal: And to Joseph it was born, two sons, before the year of the famine came, whom Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, bore to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Before the year of famine came, two sons were born to Joseph, borne to him by Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On.
verses.directors_commentary: The camera pulls in from silos to a cradle. The KJV audit starts with the clock: the Hebrew has 'the year of the famine', singular, which Radak takes to mean the first year of the famine, so 'before the years of famine came' is looser than the text. Next, the verb yulad, 'it was born', is singular, though two sons follow; the KJV's plural 'were born' evens this out. Radak wonders if they were twins, a conjecture, not a fact. 'Whom Asenath bore him' adds that both sons are hers, and Radak adds that this shows Joseph had no other wife. Her father's title carries weight: Potiphera is an Egyptian name, 'he whom Ra gave', and On is the city of the sun-god, the Greek Heliopolis, so Joseph's sons are born into the old priestly aristocracy of Egypt. Rashi quotes a Talmudic rule (Ta'anit 11a) that marital relations are barred in years of famine, hence the care to say these births came first. Rashbam links the timing to Jacob's later claim on the two sons.

philological_notes.note: 'The year of the famine', singular. Radak: the first year of the famine; the sons were born in the last of the seven good years.
Asenath, whose father's name Potiphera is Egyptian ('he whom Ra gave'). Radak: the clause 'whom Asenath bore him' means he had no other wife.

verses.translation_literal: And Joseph called the name of the firstborn Manasseh, for God has made me forget all my toil and all the house of my father.
verses.translation_dramatic: The firstborn he named Manasseh, "Making-Forget", for he said: God has made me forget it all, every hard day of my labor, and the whole house of my father.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is a name that is also a confession. Manasseh sounds like the verb nashah, 'to make forget'. Joseph, sold by his brothers and stripped of family, says God has made the toil and the father's house fade. But watch the actor's choice: 'forget' is not only relief. He names his son for the loss of his father's house, and the later chapters show that he has not truly forgotten it.

The KJV's 'toil' is fair for amal (labour, trouble, drudgery), but it adds 'said he' to supply the speaker. The form nashani is odd: Rashbam, Ibn Ezra and Radak all debate its pointing, and Radak reads Joseph as saying God gave him such wealth and honour that he forgot all his troubles and even his father's house.

philological_notes.note: The name plays on nashani, 'he made me forget'. The explanation is given by Joseph himself, not by the narrator.
Toil, trouble, labour with a sense of burden. Broader than the KJV's 'toil' alone.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] the name of the second he called Ephraim, for God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the second he named Ephraim, for God had made him fruitful in the land of his affliction.
verses.directors_commentary: The name carries the sound: Ephraim is built to echo hifrani, 'made me fruitful' (root p-r-h), the way Manasseh echoed 'made me forget'. Joseph's first name looked backward, to what was lost; this one looks at where he stands. The weight sits on the last word. The KJV's 'affliction' is accurate ('oni: affliction, humiliation); the BBE's 'sorrow' softens it. Radak glosses: the land that was at first the land of my affliction, now fruitful in children, wealth and honour. The old translations read the same word differently: Onkelos has 'servitude', Pseudo-Jonathan has 'suffering'. Say 'affliction' like a man naming the place of his humiliation, and notice that he does not leave it: he is fruitful in that same land, not in a better one. The KJV's 'caused me to be fruitful' is a fair rendering of the causative verb.

philological_notes.note: Causative of 'be fruitful': 'he made me fruitful'. The name Ephraim echoes it.
'My affliction', humiliation. Radak: the land that was first my land of affliction, now fruitful in children, wealth and honour.

verses.translation_literal: And the seven years of the plenty that was in the land of Egypt came to an end.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the seven years of plenty, the years of overflowing granaries in the land of Egypt, came to their end.
verses.directors_commentary: A plain narrative hinge, with no emotion in the Hebrew, only a bare ending. Play it as a held breath: Pharaoh's dream is now exactly on schedule. 'Plenty' (saVa') is the same word as 'fullness' or 'satiety', not just 'plenteousness' as the KJV has it; the Hebrew says the land was full-bellied. The verb vatikhlenah ('they were finished') is feminine plural, agreeing with 'years'.

token_glosses.gloss: and they came to an end

verses.translation_literal: And began seven years of the famine to come, as Joseph had said; and there was a famine in all the lands, and in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the seven years of famine began to come, exactly as Joseph had said. Hunger lay on all the lands; but in all the land of Egypt there was bread.
verses.directors_commentary: The prophecy lands. 'As Joseph had said' is the first public proof of his interpretation of the dreams. The KJV's 'dearth' is archaic for 'famine', and 'bread' (lechem) is the staple that stands for food generally. The sentence turns on a contrast: 'the lands' in the plural, but 'the land of Egypt' in the singular, and the second half is the surprise: bread. Rashbam explains it plainly: Egypt had bread because Joseph had put food in the cities. 'All the lands' is not the whole world: Ibn Ezra says the lands around Egypt's realm, and Ramban agrees, because far-off lands would have made no difference to Egypt's neighbours, adding the midrash that it was three lands: Phoenicia, Arabia and Philistia. On the form of 'they began', STEPBible parses a hiphil, while Ibn Ezra classes it as qal, from a doubled root; either way the sense is that the years began.

philological_notes.note: 'And they began'. STEPBible parses the verb as hiphil; Ibn Ezra classes it as qal, from the doubled root.
'In all the lands': the plural, set against the singular 'land of Egypt'. Ibn Ezra and Ramban both limit it to the lands around Egypt.
'Bread', food in general. Rashbam: Egypt had it because Joseph put food in the cities.

verses.translation_literal: And all the land of Egypt was hungry, and the people cried out to Pharaoh for the bread; and Pharaoh said to all Egypt: Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then hunger came to all the land of Egypt, and the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. And Pharaoh said to all of Egypt: Go to Joseph. Whatever he tells you, do.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb tsa'aq, 'cried out', is the sound of petition to a king, and the one verb here for the people's plea to the throne. The KJV's 'famished' is a good, slightly formal word for 'was hungry'; the BBE's 'in need of food' pads the plain verb. Note too that 'Egypt' is used for the people: Pharaoh speaks 'to all Egypt'. His order is a sentence of delegation: 'Go to Joseph; what he says to you, do.' Pharaoh delegates his authority to his steward, and the sentence is built like a royal decree. Radak: they were hungry because they had eaten what they stored, since they could not save for all seven years after giving a fifth to Pharaoh. Rashi (midrash): Joseph told them to circumcise; when they complained, Pharaoh pointed out that their hoarded grain had rotted at Joseph's word, so they had better obey him or die. That is a tradition, not the plain text, and you may use it only if it helps the actors.

philological_notes.note: 'Cried out', the shout of the wronged or needy appealing to a higher power; here the people to their king. Radak: they knew Joseph had stored from the fifth for the people's need.
'What he says to you, do'. In Rashi's midrash this is the line Pharaoh uses to enforce Joseph's order to circumcise, on the argument that the grain had already rotted at Joseph's word.

verses.translation_literal: And the famine was over all the face of the land; and Joseph opened all that [was] in them and sold grain to Egypt; and the famine grew strong in the land of Egypt.
verses.translation_dramatic: The famine lay over the whole face of the land. Then Joseph opened all that was kept within, and he sold grain to Egypt; and the famine grew strong in the land of Egypt.
verses.directors_commentary: Three moves in one verse: the famine spreads, Joseph opens, the famine hardens. The KJV supplies 'storehouses' where the Hebrew has only 'all that was in them' ('them' being the stores of the previous verses); Ibn Ezra and Onkelos supply the same word, so the KJV is a fair guess, but it is a guess. The verb vaiyishBor is the heart: shavar, 'to deal in grain', buying or selling. STEPBible has 'bought'; with Joseph as the seller it is 'sold', as the KJV, ASV and Webster have it, and as Rashi says, it is 'sale' here and 'purchase' in other verses. Radak adds that the qal covers both seller and buyer, and that grain is called sheber because it 'breaks' hunger. The BBE's 'for money' is added. Rashi reads 'the face of the land' as the rich. Ramban reads the order of events as: Joseph did not open the stores until the hunger was severe, while Radak says the severity came once buyers from other lands arrived. Both explain why 'grew strong' comes last.

philological_notes.note: 'And he sold grain' (the verb shavar, from sheber 'grain'). Rashi: 'sale' here, 'buying' elsewhere; Rashbam: it can mean buying food and drink, as in Isa 55:1; Radak: grain is sheber because it breaks hunger.
'The face of the land'. Rashi reads 'the face of the land' as the rich.
'And it grew strong': the famine hardens, the opposite of the plenty that was 'made' in 41:47.

verses.translation_literal: And all the earth came to Egypt to buy grain, to Joseph, for the famine was strong in all the earth.
verses.translation_dramatic: And from every side the whole earth came down to Egypt, to Joseph, to buy grain; for the famine was strong in all the earth.
verses.directors_commentary:
The chapter closes by widening the view from Egypt to the entire known world. 'All the earth' is the famine's range and the buyers' range: a single granary and a single man feed them. This sets up the arrival of Jacob's sons in chapter 42, the same journey made by all the other nations.

The Hebrew order 'came to Egypt to buy grain, to Joseph' is awkward; Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak all read it as inverted ('came to Joseph to buy'). The KJV smooths this, and also turns kol ha'aretz ('all the earth') into 'all countries', which names peoples where the Hebrew names the land. The ending '-ah' on mitzraymah is the directional suffix, 'toward Egypt'.

philological_notes.note: Egypt with the directional ending -ah, 'towards Egypt'.
Awkward word order, read as inverted by the commentators.

events.title: Pharaoh dreams of lean cows eating fat cows
events.narrative_summary: At the end of two full years Pharaoh dreams that he stands by the Nile. Seven fat cows come up and graze, then seven lean ones come up and eat them, and he wakes.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:1 'at the end of two years of days' (Rashbam: two full years; Ibn Ezra: the text does not say from what the two years run, perhaps the butler's release or Joseph's stay). 41:46 says Joseph was thirty when he stood before Pharaoh, a few hours after this dream, so I anchor on anchor.joseph_birth START with offset 30.5 years (age 30 running to its end, the audience falling inside that year), margin 6 months for the year-long span of 'thirty years old'. The two full years of 41:1 are kept as the text's own count since the butler's release but do not set the date; the Gen 39-40 chain is not used. A night dream of about 20 minutes. Tier REGNAL_YEAR for the age.
events.ancient_year_marker: At the end of two full years

events.title: Pharaoh dreams of thin ears swallowing full ears
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh falls asleep again and dreams of seven full ears on one stalk, then seven thin ears scorched by the east wind that swallow them. He wakes and knows it was a dream.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:5 'he slept and dreamed a second time': the same night, shortly after waking from the first dream, so 30 minutes after the first dream ends. Same night, so it carries the tier of the framing two-year count.

events.title: Pharaoh summons Egypt's diviners, who cannot interpret
events.narrative_summary: In the morning Pharaoh's spirit is troubled. He summons all the magicians and wise men of Egypt and tells them his dream, but none can interpret it.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:8 'in the morning': BOKER after the second dream ends. Duration of 3 hours to send for, assemble and consult the sages is an estimate.

events.title: The chief butler remembers Joseph and tells Pharaoh
events.narrative_summary: The chief butler tells Pharaoh he remembers his faults: the imprisonment with the chief baker, their dreams in one night, and the young Hebrew who interpreted them correctly.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:9 'this day': he speaks at once, as the sages fail, the same day. Anchored on the END of the failed consultation, brief speech of about 10 minutes, margin 3 hours.

events.title: Joseph is rushed from the dungeon to Pharaoh
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh sends for Joseph, and they bring him quickly out of the dungeon. He shaves, changes his clothes and comes in to Pharaoh.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:14 'they brought him hastily': same day, about 2 hours for the summons, shaving and changing, immediately after the butler's words.

events.title: Pharaoh tells Joseph his dreams
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh says no one can interpret his dream and that Joseph is said to understand dreams. Joseph answers that God will give Pharaoh an answer of peace, and Pharaoh recounts both dreams.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:15–24: a continuous audience after Joseph's arrival; the recital of both dreams takes about 15 minutes.

events.title: Joseph interprets the dreams and advises Pharaoh
events.narrative_summary: Joseph says both dreams are one: seven years of plenty will be followed by seven years of famine. He advises Pharaoh to appoint a wise man and officers to take a fifth of the harvest in the plentiful years and store it.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:25–36: the interpretation follows the recital in the same audience. About 30 minutes.

events.title: Pharaoh sets Joseph over all Egypt
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh and his servants approve the plan. Pharaoh puts Joseph over his house and all Egypt, gives him his signet ring, fine linen and a gold chain, and has him ride in the second chariot as men cry out before him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:37–44 follow in the same audience with the ceremony; I take it as the same day, about 3 hours, with a margin of a day since the text does not mark when the ceremony took place.

events.title: Pharaoh renames Joseph and gives him Asenath
events.narrative_summary: Pharaoh names Joseph Zaphenath-paneah and gives him Asenath, daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, as wife.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:45 gives no interval after the investiture; I place it two weeks after the end of the ceremony, margin two weeks. Tier REGNAL_YEAR, falling under Joseph's age of thirty in 41:46.

events.title: Joseph, thirty years old, goes out over the land of Egypt
events.narrative_summary: Joseph is thirty years old when he stands before Pharaoh. He goes out from Pharaoh's presence and travels throughout the land of Egypt.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:46 'thirty years old': anchored on the investiture END, which follows the audience dated from anchor.joseph_birth at 30.5 years (the dream chain), so the age 30 is carried by the birth-anchored chain and not absorbed by this event's margin. Duration 1 year for the circuit of the land is an estimate. Tier REGNAL_YEAR for the age.
events.ancient_year_marker: When Joseph was thirty years old

events.title: Joseph gathers grain in the cities like the sand of the sea
events.narrative_summary: Joseph collects the food of the seven years and stores it in the cities, each city's own surrounding harvest, until he stops counting.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:48–49 spans the seven years of plenty, anchored on the parent START with the same duration.

events.title: The seven years of plenty in Egypt
events.narrative_summary: In the seven plentiful years the earth brings forth abundantly. Joseph stores the grain, and two sons are born to him before the famine.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:47 'the seven plenteous years': seven years from the start of Joseph's administration (the tour starts when he leaves Pharaoh). Margin one week.

events.title: Asenath bears Manasseh
events.narrative_summary: Before the famine Asenath bears Joseph his firstborn, whom he names Manasseh, 'God has made me forget my toil and my father's house'.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:50–51: 'before the years of famine came', after the marriage (41:45). Offset 2.5 years from the start of plenty, margin 2 years: the window runs from about the first year (at least nine months after the marriage) to year 4.5, early enough that Ephraim is still born before the famine. Only the order and the 'before the famine' bound are textual. Radak reads 'in the last year of the seven' (בשנה האחרונה של השבע נולדו) for the two births; that reading would put Manasseh later than this window and is noted, not followed.

events.title: Asenath bears Ephraim
events.narrative_summary: Joseph names the second son Ephraim, 'God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction'.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:52: second son, after Manasseh and, by 41:50, before the years of famine. Offset 2.2 years from Manasseh's birth with margin 2.2 years, so the window runs from about the end of Manasseh's birth year to the last of the seven years without passing it. Only the order and the 'before the famine' bound are textual; the interval is an estimate.

events.title: The seven years of plenty end and the famine begins
events.narrative_summary: The seven years of plenty end and the years of dearth begin, as Joseph had said. There is famine in all lands, but in Egypt there is bread.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:53–54: starts when the seven years end. The first year is dated one year as its extent; the famine runs seven years, only the first year here.

events.title: The famished Egyptians cry to Pharaoh, who sends them to Joseph
events.narrative_summary: When all Egypt is famished, the people cry to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh tells them to go to Joseph and do what he says.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:55 'when all the land was famished': no interval is given. Estimated one year into the famine, as private stocks run out, margin six months; REGNAL_YEAR because it falls under the counted famine years.

events.title: Joseph opens the storehouses and sells grain to Egypt and the world
events.narrative_summary: The famine spreads over the whole earth. Joseph opens the storehouses and sells to the Egyptians, and all countries come to Egypt to buy grain from him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 41:56–57 follows Pharaoh's order and continues through the famine. Duration of one year as a minimal span; the chapters that follow date further selling (Gen 45:6, the second year).

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Joseph's accurate interpretation of the butler's dream in prison is what the butler recalls to Pharaoh (41:12–13).
Hearing of the Hebrew interpreter, Pharaoh sends for Joseph (41:14).
Only after all the sages fail does the chief butler speak up and remember his faults (41:9).
The troubling dreams make Pharaoh summon the sages of Egypt, who cannot interpret them (41:8).
The famine leaves the Egyptians hungry, so they cry to Pharaoh for bread (41:55).
The grain stored during the plenty is what Joseph sells in the famine (41:56).
The dearth begins 'according as Joseph had said' (41:54, 41:30).
Joseph's interpretation and plan please Pharaoh, who finds no one as wise and sets him over Egypt (41:37–41).
The seven years of great plenty come as Joseph said (41:29, 41:47).
Joseph's authority over the land lets him gather and store the grain of the seven years (41:48).
Pharaoh's order 'Go to Joseph' leads Joseph to open the storehouses and sell (41:55–56).

entities.canonical_name: The diviners and wise men of Egypt
entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ḥarṭummim, probably from Egyptian 'chief lector priest', scribes skilled in sacred writing and magic.
entities.summary_bio: The court's scribe-priests and sages, summoned by Pharaoh to interpret his two dreams. None of them can do it, which leads to Joseph's summoning.

entities.etymology_meaning: Hebrew ye'or, 'river', from Egyptian itrw; the text's usual word for the Nile.
entities.summary_bio: The great river of Egypt, on whose bank Pharaoh stands in his first dream and from which the cows come up. Egypt's life and harvests depend on it.

entities.etymology_meaning: Egyptian Iunu, 'pillar (city)'; the Greeks called it Heliopolis, 'city of the sun'.
entities.summary_bio: Egyptian city and centre of sun worship, where Potiphera is priest. Joseph's wife Asenath comes from it.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably Egyptian, 'she belongs to (the goddess) Neith'.
entities.summary_bio: Egyptian woman given by Pharaoh as wife to Joseph. She is the daughter of Potiphera, priest of On, and bears Joseph two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, before the famine.

entities.etymology_meaning: Folk etymology in the text: 'doubly fruitful', for God made Joseph fruitful in the land of his affliction.
entities.summary_bio: Second son of Joseph and Asenath, born in Egypt before the famine. Joseph names him in thanks for God's blessing in the land of his suffering.

entities.etymology_meaning: Folk etymology in the text: 'causing to forget', for God made Joseph forget his hardship and his father's house.
entities.summary_bio: Firstborn son of Joseph and Asenath, born in Egypt before the famine. Joseph names him for God's relief from his past suffering.

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably Egyptian, 'he whom Ra has given'.
entities.summary_bio: Priest of On (Heliopolis) and father of Asenath, whom Pharaoh gives to Joseph as wife. He appears only as her father.

components.evidence_explanation: 41:45: Pharaoh gave Joseph Asenath daughter of Potiphera as a wife.
41:9: 'I remember my faults this day' as he tells Pharaoh of the young Hebrew in prison.
41:47: 'the land produced abundantly' for seven years.
41:54: the seven years of famine began 'as Joseph had said'.
41:52: 'the name of the second he called Ephraim.'
41:40–41: all the people are to order themselves by Joseph's word, and Pharaoh sets him over Egypt, so he answers to Pharaoh alone.

systems.name: Interpretation of dreams
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In Egypt and Mesopotamia dreams were read as messages from the gods, and trained scribe-priests consulted dream books to interpret them. In Genesis the interpretation belongs to God, and a gifted person may be his channel.
rules_and_mechanics: A troubling dream is brought to recognised experts.
Doubled dreams show that the matter is fixed by God and will come soon (41:32).
Interpretation is received from God rather than produced by skill (41:16).
The interpreter also advises how to act on it.

systems.name: Royal investiture of an official
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Egyptian kings installed a vizier or favoured official by giving a signet ring, fine linen, and a gold collar, and by public proclamation. Egyptian reliefs show such 'gold of honour' presentations.
rules_and_mechanics: The king hands over his signet ring as delegated authority.
The official is clothed in fine linen and given a gold chain.
He rides in the second chariot while heralds proclaim him.
Only the throne remains above him.

systems.name: Royal renaming of a court official
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Kings in the ancient Near East gave foreign officials new local names, showing their entry into the court and the king's authority over them (compare Daniel 1:7).
rules_and_mechanics: The king gives the new name.
The new name marks incorporation into the royal household.
Often joined with a marriage into a leading local family.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Pharaoh tells the Egyptian diviners and wise men his dream, but no one can interpret it for him.
system_instances.significance_note: The failure of Egypt's experts sets up Joseph's appearance and shows that interpretation comes from God.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Seven lean cows rise from the Nile and eat seven fat cows, and Pharaoh wakes.
system_instances.significance_note: The first of two matching dreams, which Joseph later says God sent as a warning (41:25).

system_instances.outcome_summary: Seven thin, scorched ears swallow seven full ears; Pharaoh wakes and knows it was a dream.
system_instances.significance_note: The second dream repeats the first in other images, which shows the matter is settled by God (41:32).

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph explains that both dreams mean seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and advises Pharaoh to appoint a wise overseer and store grain.
system_instances.significance_note: The interpretation, credited to God, takes Joseph from prison to supreme office.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Joseph says God made him fruitful in the land of his affliction and names his second son Ephraim.
system_instances.significance_note: Joseph credits God for his blessing in exile, a name later borne by a leading tribe.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Pharaoh gives Joseph his signet ring, linen robes and a gold chain, and has him ride in the second chariot with heralds crying 'Abrek'.
system_instances.significance_note: Joseph is publicly installed as ruler under Pharaoh.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Pharaoh calls Joseph Zaphenath-paneah and gives him Asenath, daughter of the priest of On, as wife.
system_instances.significance_note: Joseph is brought into Egypt's ruling and priestly elite, which prepares his sons' place in Israel's story.
